newsitem.title: USA: Governor acts to help New York apartment renters.
newsitem.headline: Governor acts to help New York apartment renters.

text.p: New York state's 50-year-old rent laws hung in the balance Saturday as the deadline neared for their expiration and Gov. George Pataki acted to protect tenants from greedy landlords.

The regulations, which cap rent increases on 1.2 million apartments, primarily in New York City, will terminate at midnight Sunday unless state lawmakers agree on a plan to save them. Republican lawmakers want a watered-down version. Democrats want to keep the same laws and are being blamed for refusing to compromise.
Along with issuing an executive order to protect tenants if the laws lapse, the Republican governor blasted Democratic Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver for failing to negotiate a solution.

"Speaker Silver has said time and again that he would rather let the rent laws expire than compromise. That is wrong. He is wrong," Pataki said. "Mr. Silver must act responsibly and back away from his plans to kill rent protections for millions of New Yorkers on Sunday."

"I will continue to urge him to accept my plan, which protects more than 99 percent of all tenants, maintains the broad rights of succession for family members and loved ones, cracks down on dishonest landlords, and encourages more housing opportunities for all New Yorkers," the governor said.
Republican lawmakers and the governor are seeking rent decontrol for apartments once tenants move out or die, a policy known as vacancy decontrol. They also want to lower income limits from $250,000.
Democrats say vacancy decontrol will lead eventually to rent deregulation for all apartments. Silver was unavailable for comment Saturday.

Since 1994 rent laws have been either weakened or eliminated in several states, including Massachusetts and California. In 32 other states, where there have been no regulations for some time, lawmakers have passed bills to prohibit cities from adopting new laws on their own.

In New York, where the laws have remained strong until recent attacks by the Republican administration, state leaders will spend Sunday in private sessions trying to agree on details of an agreement before the deadline. Lawmakers are expected to reconvene at 8 p.m. EST Sunday.
If the Legislature passes only one-house bills, the laws will lapse, leaving more than 2 million tenants at the mercy of their landlords.

In his executive order, Pataki designated state Attorney General Dennis Vacco as a special prosecutor to investigate and prosecute cases of tenant harassment by criminal landlords along with local district attorneys.
Pataki also directed the division of Housing and Community Renewal to establish a 24-hour, toll-free hot line to handle tenant complaints about abusive landlords.
He asked that judges be temporarily assigned to housing courts in New York City and statewide to handle tenant abuse cases speedily.
